newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl faces growing resistance to reform plans.
newsitem.headline: Kohl faces growing resistance to reform plans.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, seeking dialogue with unions and opposition parties, faces a week of confrontation from outside and inside his Christian Democrat (CDU) party over controversial reforms.

Hoping to set the tone for next year's general election, Kohl's 14-year-old coalition government presented a plan last week for huge tax cuts beginning in 1999 and is now set to say how it plans to reform Germany's ailing pension system.

Kohl, trying to avoid letting the debate over the planned reforms turn into an inner-party battle and a confrontation with Germany's powerful trade unions, called for a broader dialogue with critics, unions and opposition parties.
"Let us talk about where we can make the whole thing more just," Kohl said at a campaign meeting of the Hesse state chapter of his CDU party ahead of March municipal elections.

The income tax reform cuts Germany's top tax rate to 39 percent from 53 percent. It has been sharply attacked as too little, too late from a young group of aspiring CDU politicians and has met fierce opposition from labour leaders.

The reform of the income tax code and the pension system are Germany's efforts to introduce supply-side reforms modelled after but not as far-reaching as those seen in the United States and Britain in the 1980s in a bid to boost the economy.

Trade unions such as Germany's biggest, IG Metall, or the OeTV public transport workers, white-collar DAG and the HBV banking union complained the tax reform eased burdens for the lowest and highest paid workers, but hit middle incomes hard.
"The precepts of social justice are being trampled under foot," said IG Metall's energetic chairman Klaus Zwickel at the 50th anniversary of the union's Bavarian chapter in Munich.
"We will sit down with the other unions and if there are no noticeable revisions we will consider appropriate action."
Trade unions were particularly angry over goverment plans to fully tax wages for work on Sundays, at night and on holidays, which currently are taxed at a lower rate.

Oskar Lafontaine, the firey opposition Social Democrat (SPD) party boss, said the government's income tax reform came too late, urging Kohl to bring the reform forward a year. He also rejected raising taxes on Sunday and holiday work.
"Nurses, bus drivers and people working at night must not become losers of the tax reform," he told the daily Express.

Dieter Hundt, president of Germany's BDA employers group, told the Magdeburger Volkstimme newspaper that the tax reform would boost foreign investment in Germany and be a big step towards reducing the the cost of labour.

Even as the tax discussion contiued to burn white-hot, another related debate flared up that pits Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, Kohl's longest-serving cabinet member, against Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

Bluem has taken a hard line on pension reform, demanding that unrelated costs -- such as maternity benefits, vocational training for the unemployed and payments for war victims -- be financed by taxes instead of through monthly pension payments.

In what could turn into a game of brinkmanship in cabinet this week, Bluem made clear in numerous press interviews that he would not present a pension reform plan this week unless it was clear that unrelated costs were removed from the system.
The weekly Bild am Sonntag flashed a banner headline with the question, "Will Bluem be Toppled over Pension Reform?"

The minister himself did not go so far as to threaten to step down, carefully saying in an interview with the weekly news magazine Der Spiegel, "Resigning is not something you threaten with, it is something you do."

Bluem wants to create a special "Family Fund" for these costs that would be financed by raising VAT and possibly other indirect taxes, but Waigel needs the VAT hike to finance income tax cuts. CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said he expected a solution this week along the lines of Bluem's proposals.
